lectureTitle: Course Introduction
title: Model–data feedback loop
alt: Flow diagram linking a scientific question, experimental data, a parametric model, and predictions for unseen data
caption: Fitting parameters is only the middle of the loop. A model must first predict data that were not used for fitting; systematic stimulus-dependent residuals then determine whether the hypothesis should be retained, revised, or replaced.

lectureTitle: Vectors, Matrices, and Probability
title: Conditioning a joint Gaussian shifts the mean and reduces the variance
alt: Comparison of a variable's marginal Gaussian density with its conditional Gaussian density after fixing the other variable
caption: When two variables are correlated, fixing \(X_{2}\) takes a slice through the joint density. The conditional mean shifts along the correlation direction, while conditional variance decreases from \(\sigma _{1}^{2}\) to \(\sigma _{1}^{2}(1-c^{2})\). The curves are normalized illustrations of the formula, not empirical histograms.

lectureTitle: Differential Equations and Euler Simulation
title: Exact exponential decay versus Euler approximation
alt: Comparison of the exact solution of first-order exponential decay with Euler points using a step equal to half the time constant
caption: For \(\tau dx/dt=-x\), forward Euler advances one step along the current tangent. With \(\Delta t=\tau /2\) it is stable, but at finite step size it decays faster than the exact exponential. Reducing \(\Delta t\) moves the discrete points toward the exact curve.

lectureTitle: Neurons I: Membrane Voltage, Circuits, and Integrate-and-Fire
title: Current conservation in the membrane equivalent circuit
alt: Equivalent-circuit flow diagram in which applied current splits into capacitive current and ionic-channel currents at the membrane node
caption: Node conservation divides the applied current into two parts: C \(dV_{m}/dt\) changes the charge stored across the membrane, while \(\sum G_{x}(V_{m}-E_{x})\) flows through ionic branches. \(E_{x}\) sets the zero-current voltage of a branch, and \(G_{x}\) sets how strongly that branch pulls \(V_{m}\) toward \(E_{x}\).

lectureTitle: Neurons II: LIF Solution and Hodgkin–Huxley
title: Threshold and refractoriness jointly shape the LIF F–I curve
alt: Schematic curve showing how LIF firing rate varies with input current and approaches the refractory-period limit
caption: When \(I_{e}\le I_{T}\), the subthreshold steady state cannot reach threshold, so firing rate is zero. Above \(I_{T}\), the logarithmic term in the threshold-crossing time shapes the curve, while the absolute refractory period \(\delta\) limits the strong-input rate to \(1/\delta\).

lectureTitle: Neural Coding I: Poisson Spikes and Maximum Likelihood
title: Information-compression chain from voltage traces to a PSTH
alt: Flow diagram converting a continuous voltage trace into spike times, a repeated-trial raster, and a PSTH
caption: Threshold detection first compresses a continuous trace into event times. The raster retains each trial's event structure, whereas the PSTH divides the total spike count in a time bin by \(K\Delta t\), yielding a rate averaged across trials while discarding trial identity.

lectureTitle: Neural Coding II: Population Decoding, Fisher Information, and Bayes
title: Fisher information in an independent Poisson population scales with NT
alt: Normalized diagram showing Fisher information increasing linearly with neuron count at two observation durations
caption: For uniform tuning and conditional independence, \(J\approx NTj_{f}\). Thus, with tuning shape fixed, doubling either neuron count N or observation time T doubles information, whereas asymptotic error standard deviation shrinks only as \(1/\sqrt{NT}\).

lectureTitle: Neural Networks I: Spikes, Convolution, and E/I Balance
title: A strongly coupled network retains finite fluctuations after balance
alt: Flow diagram in which many excitatory and inhibitory spikes are filtered into large opposing inputs that cancel in the net input
caption: Under \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), the conditional means of excitatory and inhibitory input are each \(O(\sqrt N)\) and must cancel at leading order. Their instantaneous difference remains \(O(1)\), so net input is not zero at every instant and can continue to drive irregular spiking.

lectureTitle: Neural Networks II: Synaptic Dynamics and Rate Models
title: The synaptic time constant determines how long one spike is retained
alt: Comparison of fast and slow exponentially decaying synaptic states with the same initial amplitude
caption: For a peak-normalized exponential response, larger \(\tau _{s}\) makes the effect of a spike decay more slowly and preserves a longer memory. Under the area-normalized kernel \(K_{s}=\tau _{s}^{-1}e^{-t/\tau _{s}}\), the peak also changes as \(1/\tau _{s}\), so the normalization convention must be checked before curves are compared.

lectureTitle: Synaptic Plasticity
title: Oja's Rule Selects the Principal Statistical Direction While Bounding Weight Norm
alt: A flow diagram in which centered input produces a linear output, a Hebbian growth term combines with Oja normalization to update weights, and the result is a bounded principal covariance mode.
caption: For centered linear input, the Oja update combines the Hebbian term h x and weight-dependent decay \(-h^{2}w\) in one local rule. The first rotates w toward high-variance directions of the input covariance, while the second strengthens as output grows, allowing the direction to approach the principal eigenvector without unbounded norm growth. This conclusion assumes stationary input, a suitably small learning rate, and a nondegenerate largest eigenvalue.

lectureTitle: Machine Learning: Regression, Gradient Descent, and Backpropagation
title: The Negative Gradient Descends the Local Loss Slope
alt: A normalized one-dimensional convex loss curve with a sequence of gradient-descent iterates approaching its minimum.
caption: At the current parameter, the gradient points in the locally fastest direction of increasing loss, so update \(\Delta w=-\eta \nabla L\) moves in the opposite direction. The markers show only normalized iteration order, not experimental observations. They illustrate that an appropriate step can approach the minimum successively, whereas the Taylor approximation does not guarantee descent with an excessively large learning rate.

lectureTitle: Introduction to Vision: Hierarchy, Receptive Fields, and LNP Models
title: From ON/OFF Local-Contrast Channels to an Oriented Gabor-Like Receptive Field
alt: A flow diagram in which a retinal image patch passes through ON- and OFF-center-surround contrast channels and spatially arranged positive and negative subregions to produce an oriented Gabor-like linear drive.
caption: ON/OFF center-surround filters first recode absolute luminance as local contrast. Arranging several polarity-specific subfields along one axis makes signed contributions add for the matching direction and cancel for an orthogonal direction, creating an elongated, orientation-selective Gabor-like linear receptive field. The diagram distinguishes local DoG contrast computation from the later subfield arrangement that creates orientation tuning.

lectureTitle: Spike-Triggered Average and White-Noise System Identification
title: Forward LNP Prediction and Reverse STA Estimation Form One Validation Workflow
alt: A flow diagram showing white-noise stimulus histories passing through a linear projection and nonlinearity to generate spikes, after which pre-spike stimuli are aligned and averaged to produce an STA parallel to the filter direction.
caption: A forward LNP model projects stimulus history onto \(L=k^{\mathrm{T}}s\), transforms it through \(F(L)\) into a conditional firing rate, and generates spikes. Reverse analysis aligns and averages the stimulus history before each spike. For zero-mean white Gaussian input, one relevant dimension, and sufficient data, STA points along k. Colored input, an even nonlinearity, or multiple relevant dimensions breaks this simple relation.

lectureTitle: Spike-Triggered Covariance and Generalized Linear Models
title: A Population GLM Places Stimulus, Self-History, and Coupling in One Conditional Predictor
alt: Three input branches represent stimulus history, a neuron's own spike history, and other neurons' histories; after filtering, they meet in a linear predictor whose inverse link produces a conditional spike probability.
caption: A population GLM adds a stimulus filter, self-history filter, and cross-neuron coupling filters in predictor \(\eta _{i}(t)\), then uses a log or logit inverse link to produce a nonnegative rate or binary spike probability. Simultaneous fitting reduces omitted-covariate confounding, but a coupling coefficient still denotes predictive dependence conditional on the included variables, not an anatomical synapse.

lectureTitle: Efficient Coding and Information Theory
title: Redundancy Reduction in a Noisy Sensory Channel Must Respect Fidelity and Output-Cost Constraints
alt: A flow diagram in which a sensory signal with input noise passes through a linear encoder and output-noise channel to a decorrelated output code jointly constrained by retained information and output cost.
caption: Encoder A transforms signal and input noise together, whereas output noise enters after A. A diagonal output covariance alone therefore does not guarantee useful coding. In the Atick–Redlich framework, redundancy is reduced subject to retained-information and output-power or dynamic-range constraints. Whitening removes second-order correlations, but any orthogonal rotation preserves whitened covariance; localized center-surround filters require additional assumptions such as symmetry and locality.

lectureTitle: Adaptation, Natural Scene Statistics, and Fourier Analysis
title: Noise Truncates the Ideal High-Frequency Gain of Natural-Image Whitening
alt: A normalized spatial-frequency plot comparing ideal linearly rising whitening gain, a noise-aware band-pass response, and a narrower low-frequency response at lower signal-to-noise ratio.
caption: If natural-image power is approximated by \(P_{\mathrm{in}}(\xi )\propto 1/|\xi |^{2}\) and noise and gain limits are temporarily ignored, flattening \(P_{\mathrm{out}}=|\hat{K}|^{2}P_{\mathrm{in}}\) requires \(|\hat{K}|\propto |\xi |\). Real optics attenuate extreme high-frequency signal without eliminating approximately flat output noise, so a noise-aware filter rolls off at high frequencies. When SNR falls further, the reliable band narrows and favors pooling. All three curves are normalized theoretical sketches, not empirical measurements.

lectureTitle: Visual Networks: Cascades, Complex Cells, and Recurrence
title: After Surround Input Shifts the I-Nullcline, Both E and I Can Fall at the Stable Intersection
alt: A normalized excitatory-inhibitory rate phase plane in which one E-nullcline intersects center and surround I-nullclines; the surround fixed point lies at lower excitatory and inhibitory rates.
caption: In a locally linear E/I rate model, a nullcline intersection is a steady state. Increasing surround drive to the I population shifts the I-nullcline upward. Its new intersection with the fixed E-nullcline can have both lower \(r_{E}\) and lower \(r_{I}\), so surround suppression does not require inhibitory firing to rise. The curves are normalized geometric sketches of the course equations. Full stability still requires Jacobian eigenvalues and cannot be inferred from line intersection alone.

lectureTitle: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
title: In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes
alt: A flow diagram that transforms population activity from neuronal coordinates through V inverse into mode amplitudes, evolves them independently in diagonal eigenvalue space, and reconstructs neuronal activity with V.
caption: If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron.

title: Scree-plot cliff and cumulative variance
alt: The normalized scree curve drops sharply and then enters a flat tail, while cumulative variance gradually approaches one hundred percent.
caption: Read the two curves in principal-component order: beyond the cliff, each eigenvalue contributes little additional variance, while cumulative variance continues to rise monotonically. The elbow suggests candidate dimensionalities but does not determine a unique cutoff; the plotted coordinates illustrate the normalized relation and are not empirical data.

lectureTitle: Population Activity and Principal Component Analysis

title: Morris–Lecar nullclines and the relaxation cycle
alt: A voltage–recovery phase plane with an N-shaped voltage nullcline, an S-shaped recovery nullcline, an unstable intersection, and a relaxation trajectory encircling that intersection.
caption: The intersection of the two nullclines is a candidate equilibrium. Here it is unstable, so the trajectory moves slowly along the outer attracting branches of the V-nullcline and jumps rapidly to the other branch near each fold. Long portions of the loop represent slow recovery, whereas nearly horizontal crossings represent fast voltage transitions. The curves are a normalized schematic of the mechanisms.
lectureTitle: Central Pattern Generators and Oscillations

title: Three fates of an eigenvalue-one integrator
alt: After the command ends, a mode whose eigenvalue is less than one decays, a mode equal to one persists, and a mode greater than one grows.
caption: After input is removed, the fate of the same initial mode amplitude depends only on \(1-\lambda\): when \(\lambda <1\) it leaks; when \(\lambda =1\) the restoring coefficient in the derivative vanishes and memory persists; when \(\lambda >1 a\) small deviation grows. Thus \(\det(I-W)=0\) guarantees only an integrating mode, and the stability of all remaining modes must still be checked.
lectureTitle: Oculomotor Integrator, Degeneracy, and Sloppy Models

title: From population activity to closed-loop BMI
alt: Population neural activity passes through GPFA latent inference, cross-day alignment, and a shared BMI decoder to produce cursor feedback, which then affects subsequent neural activity.
caption: Observed activity is first compressed by GPFA into daily latent coordinates, then \(A_{d}\) aligns those coordinates to a shared space and passes them to shared decoder B. Decoder output changes cursor feedback, which in turn changes subsequent neural activity. Cross-day stability therefore means that a low-dimensional mapping is transferable; it does not require each neuron's loading to remain fixed.
lectureTitle: Motor Cortex Latent Dynamics and Brain–Machine Interfaces

title: First-passage paths in drift–diffusion
alt: Two noisy accumulation trajectories leave the same starting point and first reach the positive and negative decision boundaries, respectively.
caption: Each path begins at bias b, accumulates noisy evidence step by step, and stops the first time it reaches +B or −B. The endpoint determines choice and the horizontal coordinate determines decision time. Under identical task parameters, noise can carry the two trajectories to different boundaries; a trajectory must not be averaged further after crossing before a decision is assigned.
lectureTitle: Short-Term Memory and Perceptual Decisions

title: TD error transfers from reward to a predictive cue
alt: Three timelines compare dopamine prediction error around the cue and reward deadline before learning, after learning, and when reward is omitted.
caption: Compare the same trial row by row. Before learning, only unexpected reward produces positive \(\delta\). After the cue–reward relation is learned, positive \(\delta\) moves earlier to the cue and is nearly zero when reward arrives on time. If reward is omitted at the deadline, negative \(\delta\) appears then. This pattern of signs supports prediction error rather than a pure reward response.
lectureTitle: Learning from Rewards

title: The agent–environment loop and a one-step Bellman backup
alt: The agent selects an action from the current state, the environment returns reward and a next state, and a one-step Bellman target updates the action value backward.
caption: In the forward interaction, policy maps \(s_{t}\) to \(a_{t}\), after which the environment samples r and \(s_{t+1}\). The backup then uses \(r+\gamma \max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')\) to update current \(Q(s_{t},a_{t})\). A dashed path carries \(s_{t+1}\) into the next cycle, showing that the Markov transition and value backup are connected steps pointing in opposite directions.
lectureTitle: Reinforcement Learning: MDPs, Bellman Equations, and Q-Learning

title: Hopfield basins: descent does not guarantee correct recall
alt: A cue near the target descends to the stored pattern under asynchronous updates, whereas an ambiguous cue lowers energy as well but descends to a spurious minimum
caption: With symmetric weights, a zero diagonal, and asynchronous updates, both paths make E nonincreasing, but the cue's basin determines the endpoint. A cue near the target can complete to \(\xi ^{\mu }\), whereas crosstalk may draw an ambiguous cue into a mixture. Low energy therefore guarantees stability, not correct recall.
lectureTitle: Hopfield Associative Memory

title: The offline replay channel in Teacher–Student–Notebook
alt: Teacher trains Student online, Student activity is stored together with a sparse Notebook code, and after Notebook completion, V reconstructs the Student pattern for offline replay.
caption: During online learning, Teacher generates training experiences, and each Student pattern \(z^{\mu }\) is stored together with its Notebook code \(\xi ^{\mu }\). During retrieval, the Notebook first completes a partial cue and then uses V to compute \(\widetilde{z}_i=\sum _jV_{ij}\xi _{j}\). The dashed replay path returns the reconstructed activity to Student, allowing Student to continue learning while Teacher is absent.
lectureTitle: Systems Consolidation and Generalization
